The same meta-analysis found the benefit reversed to a deficit at depths of 140-160 cm and 180-200 cm, with a considerable benefit only at 40-60 cm, and the benefit below a 15-degree slope was not significant [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_13, ev_soil_moisture_chen20_14]. It is a cross-site meta-analysis, not a single measured contrast. That is the villagers' own attribution across a set of villages rather than a measurement against a comparable untreated well [ev_water_access_deficit_botreij09_19].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger, planting pits in Uganda and conservation tillage with the Magoye ripper in Zambia judge the technologies to cope well with drought [ev_asset_drought_wocat_1219_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1652_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1587_2013_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1139_2013_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, not measurements, with no observed damage or failure data behind them. These are field-level practices, so the ratings describe how the treated fields fare under drought rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Heavy rain moderately damages small in-field structures. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges collapsed during heavy rain and had to be rebuilt within the season [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av]. In Morocco, staggered earth bunds are overtopped in the biggest storms and the slope gullies [ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av]. Practitioners rate zaï or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger as not coping well with local rainstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1219_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1652_2014_local_rainstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Planting pits in Uganda are rated as coping well [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1587_2013_local_rainstorm]. The Kenyan finding is a single-site trial and records rebuilding, not a size of loss [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av]; the Moroccan statement is an expert's description [ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av]; and the rest are practitioner ratings without damage records.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger not to cope well with general river floods [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1219_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1652_2014_general_river_flood].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, all from Niger, with no observed loss or failure data [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1219_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1652_2014_general_river_flood]. Pits and bunds are field-level practices, so a not-well rating describes exposure of the treated fields to floodwater rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger and planting pits in Uganda to cope well with local windstorms; no unit describes how wind would damage them [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1219_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1652_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1587_2013_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are three practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets with no observed damage data. Pits and bunds are field-level practices, so the ratings describe exposure of the treated fields rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The proximity of zai pits on crusted, degraded soil raises the chances of seed germination and dispersal, so herbaceous and woody species recolonise formerly bare land in Burkina Faso [ev_biodiversity_outcome_roose93_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_zoug14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_kabo04_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Burkina Faso evidence is descriptive, without an untreated comparison, and partly the same observation cited more than once. None of the units gives a size for the gain in species, so the strength is not quantified, and the evidence covers zai on degraded land in a single semi-arid country [ev_biodiversity_outcome_roose93_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_zoug14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_kabo04_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices store carbon in the soil as organic matter builds up where water and organic inputs are held: zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter and trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence is mixed: trenches in Mexico reduced soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso detected no significant change in organic matter even though biomass production rose [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The size of the gain rests on the Chinese figures, which come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country, and cover straw mulching and contour tillage rather than pits or trenches; the contour-tillage values are for the 5-to-10-year window with the greatest increase, not a pooled estimate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Mauritania's Sahelian watersheds, earth and stone contour bunds built to aid infiltration were followed by communities reporting rising water levels in their wells alongside improved productivity [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1]. A global review notes a few catchment-level studies have observed reduced quick runoff or increased aquifer recharge, though the authors caution these are plausible changes that cannot be generalised [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The harm side is just as real: in the Maghreb, hill-reservoir works built mechanically with large machines were found to cause a loss of cultivable land of 10 to 25% and considerably reduce the water collected downstream in the hill reservoirs [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]; and in Peru, trenches were found to have little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics dominating the outcome instead [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices that replace tillage can cut recurrent farm costs: in Mozambique labour costs were $153 per hectare for basins against $173 under conventional tillage, and mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding in an Ethiopian trial [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The savings are in recurrent costs, not the cost of building anything. Where the practice adds earthworks the cost rises: switching from flat-land production to tied ridges, with or without grass strips, increased the cost of production in Ghana's Nandom area [ev_project_cost_dalt14_2]. The Mozambique basins also carry residue retention and herbicide weed control, and the Ethiopian and Ghana statements give no cost figure [ev_project_cost_kida19_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1, ev_project_cost_dalt14_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field pits raise infiltration and water retention so crops suffer less from dry spells: zaï gave 300–400 kg of sorghum per hectare in a low-rainfall year on degraded land where the without-zaï yield was 0, only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger, zaï trials let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils with honourable yields in rainfall-deficit periods, and chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s, ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in conservation agriculture meta-analyses report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks where soil water storage reaches 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. Conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect on maize in a Kenyan season with a failed start, and a cited study reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The strongest results are practitioner-reported contrasts from a single Sahelian report, and the conservation agriculture dry-year findings are secondary citations inside meta-analyses rather than pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-situ water harvesting such as planting basins and ridge reinforcement raises soil infiltration so crops can draw on stored moisture when rains fail. In Zimbabwe, conservation-agriculture plots using planting basins improved maize yields both in above-average rainfall and during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3], and improved sorghum and cowpea yields during times of drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. In semi-arid and dry sub-humid East Africa, conservation-farming systems using ripping or pitting with fertiliser showed their largest yield advantage in rainy seasons with low and poorly distributed rainfall, by maximising infiltration so crops could bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: In southern Malawi during the 2015/16 El Nino drought, 'banking' (ridge reinforcement while crops are growing) cut yields from 245 kg per hectare to 153 kg per hectare, a 37.6% reduction, and lowered the odds of a farm meeting the maize-yield threshold for food security from 0.12 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. In Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture overall showed no specific impact in mitigating losses from either rainfall shortfalls or surpluses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 1 source. The Zimbabwe tied-ridge result is a single trial season, measures soil moisture only and gives no yield figure [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover (a soil-cover mulch, modelled separately from the other practices) raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. In Nigeria, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch raised sorghum grain yield over the flat bed by 67% in 1999 [ev_crop_yield_chir06_6], and in Malawi maize under conservation agriculture produced 700 kg per hectare more grain than conventional practice in 2015/16 [ev_crop_yield_seti18_1]. In a Zimbabwean on-farm trial, dead-level contour ridges on silt loam still held significantly more soil moisture than an adjacent plot without ridges after a dry spell lasting 3 weeks (10.4 against 9.2 mm) [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_2]. In the same 2007 dry-spell season on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, zaï planting pits alone raised grain yield by 69 percent, adding more than 300 kilograms of cereal per hectare over the untreated control [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_7].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm, so it does not address seasonal drought [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In Mozambique no cowpea yield was obtained on any treatment in a season heavily affected by drought [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2]. The Malawi on-farm survey of ground cover gives measured support, while the zaï and tassa yield contrasts are author estimates [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. In the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The Nigerian ridging gain bundles the tied ridges with mulch [ev_crop_yield_chir06_6]. The Zimbabwe contour-ridge result is soil moisture after one mild dry spell at one site, not a yield or a drought-season contrast [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_2]. That zaï contrast comes from a project table of cited yield gains with no significance test reported, so it adds size rather than certainty [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_7].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Burkina Faso, zai planting pits raised sorghum yields from nothing to 300–400 kg per hectare in a low-rainfall year, up to 1500 kg per hectare in a good year [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s]; a review states zai can reduce the impact of a drought lasting two to three weeks, provided the soil can store at least 50 mm of water [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Ethiopian rift valley, maize plots without mulch were particularly affected by dry spells, while mulched plots were not [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: At two more arid Kenyan sites, conservation-farming plots still recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four experimental seasons respectively, with average seasonal yields ranging from 2.1 to 3.7 tonnes per hectare in the seasons that did produce a harvest [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits concentrate runoff into the root zone, so crops can ride out a dry spell of two to three weeks. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: An expert statement from Burkina Faso, explicitly conditional on the soil having sufficient water storage capacity [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1], and an Ethiopian field observation of which plots wilted in dry spells, not a tested contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A global review of infiltration trenches across mountain regions found they reduced runoff by 46.4% on average, equivalent to 5.7% of rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. In Burkina Faso, a review states that combining permeable contour micro-dams (stone lines, hedges, grass strips) with zai planting pits reduces flood risk during the largest storms [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: No evidence here covers conditions more severe than this: the pool reports no measured results at severe or extreme flood, so the strong class should not be read as holding beyond the storms these structures were tested against.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A global review of infiltration trenches across mountain regions found they reduced runoff by 46.4% on average, equivalent to 5.7% of rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. In Burkina Faso, a review states that combining permeable contour micro-dams (stone lines, hedges, grass strips) with zai planting pits reduces flood risk during the largest storms [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: No evidence here covers conditions more severe than this: the pool reports no measured results at severe or extreme flood, so the strong class should not be read as holding beyond the storms these structures were tested against.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Burkina Faso, a review states that combining permeable contour micro-dams with zai planting pits reduces flood risk during the largest storms [ev_flood_hazard_roose17_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single expert assertion with no measured data behind it, so a second independent source or a measured finding is needed before this cell can state a class.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Planting basins and ground cover hold rain where crops grow, raising staple harvests. Planting basins (zai pits) raised the odds of a Kenyan plot meeting the household maize requirement to 421.75 against 1.67 in the control, and ground cover raised those odds in Malawi's El Nino season [ev_food_security_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Practice choice and season matter. In the same Malawian El Nino season, banking lowered the odds of meeting the maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054, so a mis-matched in-field practice can deepen food shortfall [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The large Kenyan odds come from an above-average rainfall season and do not show performance in drought [ev_food_security_boil19_2]. Every unit comes from the same study, a plot-level analysis of yield thresholds rather than a household food-security survey, which is why the strong class stands on a narrow base.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-situ structures like planting basins and pits raise yields mainly by holding more rainwater where the crop can use it. In Zambia, conservation farming using planting basins plus lime raised yields by 68% against a comparator where timely conventional farming alone achieved 50% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], and a separate Zambian study found conservation farming could raise maize and cotton yields by around 40% through earlier planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]. A review of Ethiopian conservation practices found stone bunds adding 321.7 kg per hectare to grain yield on average [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: In-situ structures can also underperform or backfire: at a semi-arid Kenyan site, pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment of all, below even the conventional-tillage control (1.2 versus 1.6 tonnes per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9]; and in Zimbabwe, conservation agriculture on its own was found to decrease maize yields with no significant advantage for other crops [ev_crop_yield_mich19_2], and to have no significant impact on any crop in an average-rainfall year [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 5 sources.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits, planting pits, contour bunds and planting basins can raise farm income by raising yields. Returns to labour for these practices in Burkina Faso exceed the shadow wage, and bunds show returns above cost at subproject level in Mauritania [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1, ev_economic_return_mrt14_5]. In Zimbabwe, first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots in the low-rainfall budget, with 866.84 against 357.16 for experienced farmers in high rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]. Zambian crop budgets give hand-hoe conservation-farming basins returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional plowing for cotton, and returns to land and peak-season labor 60 to 90 percent higher than hand hoe tillage for maize [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. In Zambia, partial budgets found it profitable for a household to switch to conservation agriculture, with a marginal rate of return of 860% from hand hoeing to basin digging and 360% from ploughing to basin digging [ev_economic_return_umar12_2, ev_economic_return_umar12_3]. In Mozambique basins returned $148 per hectare against $104 under conventional tillage, an imputed value of $44 per hectare for a risk-neutral farmer [ev_economic_return_kida19_2, ev_economic_return_kida19_4]. In Ghana tied ridges with grass strips gave a higher net return than flat-land maize in 2010 despite a slightly higher cost [ev_economic_return_dalt14_3], and in Nigeria wood-shavings mulch on a flat bed was expected to increase the financial benefits to farmers by 238% [ev_economic_return_chir06_11]. Further figures from the same CILSS Sahel synthesis: in Niger, the internal rate of return on zaï pits was 82 percent where the farmer rehabilitated land he already owned, falling to 39 percent where he bought degraded land to rehabilitate, still a quick payback [ev_economic_return_botreij09_26]; on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, zaï planting pits returned an internal rate of 93 percent [ev_economic_return_botreij09_32].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence conflicts, and what pulls it apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. Other losses are season- or practice-specific: tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, where net benefits were higher without it, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial, which ran at a loss of −98 624 FCFA per hectare against the experiment's own investment cost [ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. Manual zai gives far smaller net benefits than mechanised zai [ev_economic_return_zoug14_1]. The Zimbabwe margins include manure and fertiliser and the high-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]; the Zambian returns are bundled with early planting and purchased inputs, which the authors say dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]; and the Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue with labour unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The newer field trials split the same way, and cost is what separates them: in Nigeria the high production costs of open and tied ridging, with or without mulch, gave net economic losses of about 1, 0.5, 11 and 12%, while mulch on the flat bed paid [ev_economic_return_chir06_10, ev_economic_return_chir06_11]; and in Mozambique basin and conventional returns did not differ significantly at intermediate elevation [ev_economic_return_kida19_3]. The Zambian rates of return come from partial budgets of a single crop, maize. Farm income and returns are proxies for poverty. Both are internal-rate-of-return figures with no significance test and no band rule for strength, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the other currency figures in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_26, ev_economic_return_botreij09_32].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Soil and water conservation structures cut both runoff and the soil it carries. A review of Ethiopian studies found graded soil bunds reducing surface runoff by 25.2% (from 190.7 to 142.7 mm) and soil loss by 59% (from 43.6 to 17.9 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1]; level soil bunds cut runoff by 60.1% and soil loss by 88% (from 17.5 to 2.1 tonnes per hectare) [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2]; and stone bunds raised runoff reduction further still at 55.8% in a wider sample [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_4].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice worsening this outcome for some adopters — appears in 1 source.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field bunds reduce what leaves the field in runoff: an Ethiopian synthesis finds graded soil bunds reduced the loss of soil organic matter by up to 52%, total nitrogen by up to 48% and available phosphorus by up to 41% [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Confidence is very low because the row rests on a single synthesis for a single practice, graded soil bunds in the Ethiopian highlands, so the large reduction cannot be checked against any other source [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1]. The figures are upper bounds of nutrient loss from the field, not measured water chemistry downstream, and they say nothing about pits, basins or mulch. A project concerned with nutrient export downstream has one measured practice to go on.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Pits, basins, bunds and tied ridges catch rain where it falls and hold it in the root zone. A meta-analysis finds infiltration pits have the highest SMD of 114.4% for soil moisture retention, with tied ridging at 48.9% [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_2, ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_5]. In Burkina Faso zaï can retain moisture in the soil for seven to ten days after rainfall [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]; in Brazil tied furrows kept more soil moisture than the traditional flat system at all crop stages and depths [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]; and in Ethiopia hand-dug planting basins held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at flowering (27.4 against 25.5) and at maturity (26.5 against 25.9) [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_6]. Mulching, the soil-cover form of in-situ water harvesting, improves soil moisture retention with an SMD of 54.0% in the meta-analysis, and maize-stalk mulch in Ethiopia held more topsoil water than unmulched plots at Ziway at each stage measured [ev_soil_water_retention_tefe24_4, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_3, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_5]. Water productivity, the grain produced per unit of rain, is a route by which capture eases water stress. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, lifted maize rain water productivity from 3.10 kg per hectare per mm under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea to 6.61 [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In a Nigerian field trial, tied ridging with wood-shavings mulch stored 8, 26 and 14.4% more soil water than the flat bed in successive seasons, and raised rainfall water use efficiency of sorghum grain from 1.26 to 1.97 kg per hectare per mm [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_9]. Reviews cite tied ridging, open ridging and sub-soiling improving root-zone soil water by 24%, 15% and 3% over traditional tillage in drought-stricken Wollo, Ethiopia (McHugh et al., 2007), tied ridges cutting surface runoff by about 60% and raising rooting-zone soil water by at least 13% in northern Ethiopia (Araya and Stroosnijder, 2010), and 20–25 cm deep contour furrows increasing soil moisture and shrub productivity on rangeland in Iran's Sistan Baluchistan (Jahantigh and Pessarakli, 2009) [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_6, ev_soil_moisture_dile13_1, ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_8, ev_soil_moisture_stav20_6]. In a Zimbabwean on-farm trial, dead-level contour ridges on silt loam held significantly more soil moisture than an adjacent plot without ridges shortly after a 60 mm rainfall day (14 against 12.1 mm) and after a dry spell lasting 3 weeks (10.4 against 9.2 mm) [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_1, ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_2]. The Chinese terracing meta-analysis confirms soil-water-storage effectiveness across all six terrace types studied [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_2]. In a Zimbabwean cotton trial in the 2018–2019 drought season, tied contour ridges held significantly more moisture in the top 0–5 and 6–10 cm of soil than conventional tillage, though not at 11–15 cm [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Tillage alone is not water harvesting: in the Brazilian trial deep ploughing, a tillage practice, scored as high as the tied furrows [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. The Brazilian trial ran a single season at a station of the agency that promotes the technology [ev_soil_water_retention_brito07_9]. At Melkassa the Ethiopian mulch plots differed from unmulched plots only at maturity, not at planting or flowering [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_7, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_9, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_11]. The Ethiopian basins did not differ from unmulched plots at planting at Ziway or at any stage at Melkassa [ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_2, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_8, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_10, ev_soil_water_retention_sime15h2_12]. Under meteorological drought and dry spells in Kenya, tied ridging without organic inputs was insufficient in soil moisture conservation since there was little or no rainwater to be held in the basins [ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. A review found no significant effect of infiltration trenches on soil moisture because only four studies provided sufficient statistical data [ev_soil_water_retention_locat20_1]. The zaï result comes with compost in the pits [ev_soil_water_retention_sawa11h1_8]. The Mauritanian well-level and Andean trench evidence now sits in the in-situ catchment water yield row, which also answers what upstream capture does to water downstream. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers a single season, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gain belongs to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (4.84 against 3.10) were not significantly different from the control, and at Péni neither grass strips with zaï (4.51) nor earth bunds with contour ploughing (4.31) differed significantly from the control (3.53), the authors stating that water was not limiting at Péni, which had more rain than Houndé that season [ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. In the Nigerian trial, open and tied ridging without mulch stored only a few per cent more soil water, significant on only one out of the nine measurement dates, and did not consistently raise water use efficiency, so ridging may not be an improvement without a residue mulch [ev_soil_moisture_chir06_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_chir06_8]. The Ethiopian and Iranian soil-moisture figures are cited second-hand. On the sandy field of the same Zimbabwe trial, where little runoff was generated, the ridges made no significant difference to soil moisture after heavy rain or after the dry spell [ev_soil_moisture_mhiz13_3]. That is a meta-analysis finding for terracing structures specifically, not an in-situ-family measurement [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_2]. The Zimbabwe tied-ridge trial covers one drought season and found no difference in the deeper soil layer [ev_soil_moisture_mand21_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the humid Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where daily rains exceed 80 mm, zaï pits concentrate infiltration and sorghum in the pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments, whose waterlogged plants had yellow leaves and stunted growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. In Tanzania, tied ridges that helped maize in years of near-normal rainfall (500–600 mm) caused waterlogging in wet years (700–900 mm) (Jensen et al. 2003, cited in a review) [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, with no magnitude [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Ethiopian waterlogging finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser; because it comes from using the practice at a wetter site than it suits, it is held out of the production classes as an envelope misfit (a suitability caveat) and counted here as waterlogging evidence [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. The Tanzanian finding is cited second-hand and gives no yield loss [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices hold water where the crop grows, which backfires in wet conditions: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rainfall exceeds 80 mm per day and 1 200 mm per year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields because of frequent soil waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. Biazin et al. cite Jensen et al. (2003) from Tanzania: tied ridges helped maize in years of near-normal (500–600 mm) rainfall, but in wet years (700–900 mm) the maize showed waterlogging effects [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: None of the harm sources gives a magnitude. The Cameroon zaï losses come from using the practice outside its rainfall window; under the standing ruling they are held out of the production classes as performance caveats, and are counted here as waterlogging hazard evidence [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, the Tanzanian tied-ridge result is cited from an earlier study with no yield loss stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_biaz12_15], and the Cameroon result rests on that one observation [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. Most units carry no farming-system tag, so the rainfed reading rests largely on the practices being field-crop techniques.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for zaï or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger rate wind velocity as reduced [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1219_2014_wind_velocity, ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1652_2014_wind_velocity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner ratings without stated reasoning, and the Philippine conservation-tillage compiler rates wind velocity as unchanged [ev_windbreak_protection_wocat_1021_2011_wind_velocity]. water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger rate both technologies as coping well with drought [ev_asset_drought_wocat_1613_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1614_2014_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings from Niger with no observed damage data, so the row reflects compiler judgement for a single country.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger as not coping well with local rainstorms and the Vallerani system in Burkina Faso as coping moderately [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1613_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1614_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1528_2012_local_rainstorm].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are practitioner ratings without damage records, and the compiler for mechanised Vallerani harvesting in Jordan rates coping with flash floods as very good, so the outcome may depend on setting [ev_asset_flood_wocat_5860_2021_flash_flood].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The WOCAT compiler for mechanised Vallerani micro water harvesting in Jordan rates the technology as coping very well with extreme winter conditions [ev_asset_frost_wocat_5860_2021_extreme_winter_conditions].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single practitioner rating with no observed damage [ev_asset_frost_wocat_5860_2021_extreme_winter_conditions].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Burkina Faso the 2- and 3-m half-moon plots showed lower infiltration than the control plots, likely due to suspended matter that clogs the soil during sedimentation [ev_soil_permeability_zour25h1_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is one source and one trial, and the finding is for the larger (2- and 3-m) half-moons only. The authors give sedimentation as the likely cause without testing it, and the damage is reduced infiltration capacity inside the basin rather than a breach or loss of the structure [ev_soil_permeability_zour25h1_8].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate Nardi or Vallerani trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger as coping well with local windstorms, and the Vallerani system in Burkina Faso as coping very well [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1613_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1614_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1528_2012_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner ratings without observed damage.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: For the Vallerani System of tractor-ploughed micro-catchments in Burkina Faso, the WOCAT compiler reports floral diversity rising from 14 to 44 species with a high share of good forage grasses and the return of more leguminous species, an average of 14 woody species per hectare on implemented sites against 6 on control plots, and insects, birds, reptiles and mammals observed on implemented sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_animal_diversity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is data deficient: both units come from a single technology sheet compiled by a practitioner, with no independent ecological survey or description of how the control plots were chosen, and no other source or country is covered [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_plant_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1528_2012_animal_diversity]. A second independent source or one measured finding is needed before this row can state a direction or size.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchment structures (fish-scale pits, micro-basins, trenches) concentrate scarce rainfall around planted trees or vegetation, building up soil carbon and biomass. A Burkina Faso practitioner rating found biomass production on treated sites increased 5 to 30 times compared with nearby unploughed soil, averaging 1000 to 1200 kilograms of dry matter per hectare against 70 to 110 on control plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C]. A meta-analysis of Chinese studies found fish-scale pits raised soil organic carbon storage on the Loess Plateau by 79.86% over 11 to 30 years, with terracing raising it by 14.11% to 60.96% over the same period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This benefit does not guarantee tree establishment. In an Ethiopian on-farm trial, micro-basins and trenches around newly planted tree seedlings showed no significant difference in survival compared with untreated control seedlings across three tree species; the authors attributed this null result to dry-season moisture scarcity too severe for the structures to bridge, together with insect and termite attack and browsing by free-grazing livestock [ev_establishment_survival_kinuthia20_1]. The evidence base is thin, three sources across Burkina Faso, China and Ethiopia, so this picture rests on a small, specific set of measurements rather than a broad literature.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The micro-catchment family now has two per-hectare establishment-cost sources for mechanised Vallerani micro-catchment water harvesting in Jordan, both upper-middle income: the compiler's table for a floodplain trenching setup [ev_project_cost_wocat_5860_2021_establishment] and an average build cost of 20-30 US dollars per hectare cited from two other studies [ev_project_cost_tats21_3].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both sources are from the same country and income band (Jordan, upper-middle income), so the row still lacks an independent lower-income confirmation; the newer figure is itself a second-hand citation and covers only mechanised bund construction, not the seedlings or fencing established alongside it [ev_project_cost_tats21_3]. A cost source from a low- or lower-middle-income country is still needed before the row can say whether the cost is small or large.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The only evidence is a Kenyan field trial in which ridge-furrow rain harvesting with plastic film raised the value of total inputs by 89.9 and 94.1% over flat planting, because of extra labour and the purchase of plastic sheet [ev_project_cost_mo17_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: With no independent source to compare against, agreement cannot be judged; this is a thin signal rather than a settled finding. The cost rise is for ridges covered with plastic film, which is not nature-based, and the trial does not separate the cost of the film from the labour of building the ridges [ev_project_cost_mo17_8]. Cost data for micro-catchments without plastic, such as demi-lunes or Vallerani basins, would be needed to say whether the practice itself raises or lowers farm costs.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Demi-lunes — crescent-shaped earth bunds that capture runoff from a small catchment — raised grain yields by 112% over untreated fields on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau in 2007 [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_6]. A review describes the same structures as doubling infiltrated water by capturing runoff over 10 to 20 square metres, allowing crops to resist dry periods of 2 or 3 weeks [ev_drought_hazard_roose17_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: No evidence here covers conditions more severe than this: the pool reports no measured results at severe or extreme drought, so the strong class should not be read as holding beyond the dry spells these structures were tested against.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In Burkina Faso, a project reported that increased biodiversity, vegetation cover, soil fertility and water storage in the soil profile increase the whole ecosystem's resilience to drought: during years of extreme drought, plants reduced their growth but most survived and started growing again the following rainy season [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_drought_impacts]. A review describes demi-lunes as doubling infiltrated water by capturing runoff over 10 to 20 square metres, allowing crops to resist dry periods of 2 or 3 weeks [ev_drought_hazard_roose17_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence pool here is limited to these two sources, so the moderate class should be read as indicative rather than well established.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The Vallerani compiler in Burkina Faso keeps the treated area open to regulated grazing to reduce the grass growth that could favour the spread of fire, and herders monitor the area [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_fire_risk].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is data deficient: one compiler rating, not a measurement, and the reduction it describes comes from grazing management and community monitoring alongside the micro-catchments, so it is a bundled effect rather than one of the basins themselves [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_fire_risk]. A second independent source or one measured finding is needed before this row can state a direction or size.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchments retain rain where it falls; the Burkina Faso compiler for the micro-basins reports that through water harvesting the rain is retained in the precipitation area and flood risk decreases [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Data deficient: the row rests on one WOCAT compiler rating, not a measurement, and the same compiler adds that a flood in the ploughed area before vegetation is well established can wash out the micro basins [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts]. What is missing is a second independent source or a measured runoff, peak-flow or flood-damage contrast for micro-catchments; until then no class is stated, which is not the same as no effect.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Through water harvesting the rain is retained in the precipitation area and flood risk decreases, as the compiler of the Vallerani System sheet in Burkina Faso puts it [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Data deficient: the row rests on a single practitioner judgement from a technology sheet with no hydrological measurement, and the same compiler cautions that a flood on ploughed land before vegetation is established can wash out the micro basins [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_flood_impacts]. What is missing is a second independent source or a measured runoff or peak-flow contrast for micro-catchments; the absence of a class does not mean the practice has no effect on flooding.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Vallerani tractor-ploughed micro-catchments collect runoff for fodder and crops. The Burkina Faso compiler writes that food security improves with increased and diversified productivity and income, and that even in severe drought some sown plants can serve as emergency food for people and animals, while the deep root system of the sown plants and higher soil moisture and fertility reduce the risk of production failure [ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_risk_of_production_failure].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This cell is data deficient, not a finding of no effect: both units come from a single WOCAT technology sheet for Burkina Faso and are practitioner ratings, and no study measures household food security for micro-catchment practices. A second independent source, or any measured result on food security or production-failure risk, would let the cell state a class [ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_food_security_selfsufficiency, ev_food_security_wocat_1528_2012_risk_of_production_failure].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Semi-circular bunds, Vallerani micro-catchments and half-moons harvest runoff for crops and grasses. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost gave 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. A review tabulates crop yield increases of 50–200% from half-moons in Burkina Faso and Niger, and cites micro-basin water harvesting in Zambia doubling maize yields to 3 t per hectare [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. Negarim micro-catchments with supplementary irrigation supported fruit production at Embrapa Semi-Arid in Brazil, and semi-circular bunds raised millet grain production under African conditions [ev_crop_yield_fao13c_2, ev_crop_yield_fao13c_1]. For the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso the WOCAT compiler reports more fodder in quantity and quality, a surplus of 22–106 grazing days per tropical cattle unit per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1528_2012_animal_production]. A ridge-furrow micro-catchment trial found the single-ridge treatment yielded more on average than no ridging, though not significantly so [ev_crop_yield_wang07_1]. The same synthesis adds two demi-lunes measurements: in Niger's Tahoua region, demi-lunes raised millet yield 78 percent over the Illéla sub-prefecture average [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_15], and in a 2007 dry-spell season on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, demi-lunes raised grain yield 112 percent, adding at least 800 kilograms of cereal per hectare over the untreated control [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Animal production was rated lower on the Niger sheets because treated rangeland must be protected from grazing for the first years while vegetation establishes [ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1613_2014_animal_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1614_2014_animal_production]. The Burkina Faso half-moon contrast is against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so it measures bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. The FAO manual cites earlier work, the review figures are ranges and single citations rather than pooled estimates, and the WOCAT units are practitioner judgements [ev_crop_yield_fao13c_1, ev_crop_yield_fao13c_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. Two readings from the same trial pool found no effect: water-use efficiency did not differ significantly between some ridge widths and the control, and in a Jordanian micro-catchment bund system topsoil nitrogen did not differ significantly from the untreated interspace [ev_rain_water_productivity_wang07_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_tats21_2]. Both are project-table or synthesis citations with no significance test reported [ev_crop_yield_botreij09_15, ev_crop_yield_botreij09_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Vallerani tractor-ploughed micro-catchments, half-moons and ridge-furrow systems collect runoff for crops and sown fodder. In a Kenyan field trial, ridge-furrow rain harvesting raised wheat net income by 82% without mulch and 117% with straw mulch over flat planting [ev_economic_return_wang16_3, ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost were profitable at 377 275 FCFA per hectare after the investment [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3]. The Burkina Faso compiler for the Vallerani system links more and better fodder to improved animal health, productivity and market price, and so to higher farm income [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income]. The same synthesis gives an internal rate of return of 145 percent for demi-lunes on Burkina Faso's Central Plateau [ev_economic_return_botreij09_31].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The gains are per-hectare net incomes from field trials, not measured changes in household income or poverty, which they stand in for. The Kenyan figures come from one trial, and the larger wheat gain also carries a straw mulch [ev_economic_return_wang16_4]. The row rests on three sources, one of them a technology-sheet rating; measured household income for micro-catchments is missing. The half-moon profit comes from a trial on degraded land where the authors count the experiment's own investment, and compost was added to the pits [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3]. The Vallerani unit is a technology-sheet rating [ev_household_income_wocat_1528_2012_farm_income]. That is an internal-rate-of-return figure with no significance test, read ordinally rather than compared in absolute terms with the other currency figures in this row [ev_economic_return_botreij09_31].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchments trap runoff in small basins, which the Kenyan compiler says cuts the kinetic energy of rainwater and so reduces soil loss; for the Vallerani tractor-ploughed basins in Burkina Faso the compiler adds that ploughing along the contour collects the runoff flowing between the tilled lines, and that soil loss falls through runoff reduction and less wind erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_2895_2017_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1528_2012_surface_runoff, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_soil_loss].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Confidence is only medium because the row rests on practitioner ratings from the Burkina Faso and Kenyan WOCAT technology sheets; no literature measurement of soil loss covers this family, and the rated reduction says nothing about how much sediment leaves the treated area [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1528_2012_soil_loss, ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_2895_2017_soil_loss].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The Jordan sheet for mechanised Vallerani micro water harvesting rates downstream siltation as reduced, consistent with runoff and sediment being held in the micro-basins [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5860_2021_downstream_siltation].

Siltation is a component proxy for water quality; no water-quality measurement exists for this family.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Micro-catchments concentrate a small basin's runoff onto a planted pit or furrow. In Ethiopia's eastern drylands, plots with micro-catchments had 31% higher soil moisture in the wet season and 24% higher in the dry season than plots without them [ev_soil_moisture_biaz12_1]. A Chinese meta-analysis found fish-scale pits (a micro-catchment structure) raising soil-water storage by 8.9%, the smallest of six terracing-family structures tested, with level ditches reaching 34.9% [ev_soil_moisture_chen20_7]. In Burkina Faso, a project reported that its micro-basins harvest up to 95% of the rain falling on them, with each micro-basin collecting up to 1,200 litres per rainfall and each hectare collecting an average of 360,000 litres of rain and runoff combined, and that local people report rising well-water levels since the structures were installed [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1528_2012_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1528_2012_water_quantity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: In a Chinese potato trial, however, no difference in water-use efficiency was found between ridge-and-furrow micro-catchment plots and flat planting averaged over two seasons [ev_rain_water_productivity_wang07_4].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The WOCAT compiler for mechanised Vallerani micro water harvesting in Jordan rates the impacts of cyclones and rain storms as decreased, with no comment explaining why [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_wocat_5860_2021_impacts_of_cyclones_rain_storms].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is data deficient: a single compiler rating with no comment or measurement, from an upper-middle-income country outside the target band, and it concerns rain-storm impacts rather than wind [ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_wocat_5860_2021_impacts_of_cyclones_rain_storms]. A second independent source or one measured finding is needed before this row can state a direction or size.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Rooftop storage depends on rain to refill: in great multi-year droughts the domestic cistern runs dry and households fall back on water trucks, and WOCAT compilers for rooftop systems in Nepal and Uganda rate the technology as not coping well with drought [ev_drought_hazard_arsky20_3, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1497_2011_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1595_2013_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a functional failure of storage rather than structural damage; the Brazilian unit is an implementer interview and the others are practitioner ratings, none quantified [ev_drought_hazard_arsky20_3].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate rooftop rainwater systems in Nepal and Uganda as coping well with local rainstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1497_2011_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1595_2013_local_rainstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings without observed damage or stated reasoning.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate rooftop rainwater systems in Nepal and Uganda as coping well with river floods [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1497_2011_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1595_2013_general_river_flood].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings without damage records or stated reasoning.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers rate rooftop rainwater systems in Nepal and Uganda as coping well with local windstorms [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1497_2011_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1595_2013_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings without observed damage or stated reasoning.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The compiler of a WOCAT sheet on Rubagano rooftop rainwater harvesting with a concrete or brick tank in Uganda rated plant diversity slightly increased; the sheet gives no mechanism.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: A single practitioner judgement without comment or measurement; the link from roof-water storage to wider plant diversity is not explained in the source, so the row is indicative only.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Domestic rooftop cisterns in semi-arid Brazil store rainwater for the dry period, giving households basic drinking and cooking water near the home, cutting the time spent fetching water and postponing or avoiding the shortages that send families to water trucks [ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_1, ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_1, ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_4]. In a survey of beneficiary families, 57.8% said the cistern fully met drinking, cooking and personal hygiene needs, and the WOCAT compiler for a rooftop tank system in Uganda rates water quantity and availability as improved [ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_2, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1595_2013_water_quantity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The benefit is set by storage per person: a 16 thousand-litre cistern gives a family of four 16.6 litres per person-day, larger households stay dependent on water trucks, and only 19.1% of surveyed families named the cistern as their main source [ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_2, ev_water_access_deficit_brito07_1, ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_2]. In great multi-year droughts the cisterns run dry and households fall back on water trucks, which records no benefit at that point rather than damage to the tank [ev_drought_hazard_arsky20_3]. The survey used recall with no control group, the other Brazilian units are implementer or author statements, and the Ugandan units are practitioner ratings; all describe domestic water access as a component proxy, not crop or livestock losses [ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_1, ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Domestic cisterns in semi-arid Brazil store rainwater for the dry season, but in great multi-year droughts they run dry and households fall back on water trucks, leaving them very vulnerable [ev_drought_hazard_arsky20_3].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single expert statement from a Brazilian programme account, upper-middle-income and adjacent to the target; it records no drought benefit once storage is exhausted, a benefit shortfall rather than damage to the tank, and says nothing about shorter droughts.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The pooled cost is the average construction cost of a roof rainwater-harvesting tank under the Himachal Pradesh mid-Himalayan watershed project in India, reported per structure from the project's output table.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: A single lender completion report, self-reported from physical and financial monitoring; the figure is a nominal rupee average over the project years converted at one exchange rate, so it indicates the order of cost of a household tank rather than a transferable unit rate.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Rooftop tanks capture part of the rain falling on roofs; the WOCAT compiler for a rooftop system with a concrete or brick tank in Uganda rates surface runoff and downstream flooding as reduced [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1595_2013_surface_runoff, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1595_2013_downstream_flooding].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both sheets are practitioner ratings, and the Nepal compiler rates downstream flooding as unchanged because only a little portion of rainfall is trapped from the roof [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1497_2011_downstream_flooding].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Rooftop systems trap part of the rainfall from roofs, and the compiler for Rubagano rooftop harvesting with a concrete or brick tank in Uganda judged downstream flooding slightly reduced.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Only practitioner judgements from technology sheets; the Nepal compiler rated the effect neutral because only a little rainfall is trapped from the roof, so any flood benefit is marginal.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The only unit is the compiler's rating on the WOCAT sheet for the Rubagano rooftop rainwater harvesting system with a concrete or brick tank in Uganda, which records crop production as increased; the sheet gives no comment on how the stored roof water reaches crops [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1595_2013_crop_production].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a practitioner judgement from a documented technology sheet, not a measured yield, and no literature unit supports it; whether the rating holds beyond this single Ugandan technology is untested [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1595_2013_crop_production].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The Ugandan Rubagano rooftop system's WOCAT sheet rates farm income and food self-sufficiency as increased [ev_household_income_wocat_1595_2013_farm_income, ev_food_security_wocat_1595_2013_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Brazil, domestic cisterns fully met family drinking and household needs for many households and improved quality of life and health, but did not influence income [ev_household_income_silva09_3].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The signals point in different directions: a Brazilian household survey from an upper-middle-income setting finds no income effect, while the Ugandan input is a single compiler's ratings that also record the risk of production failure as unchanged [ev_household_income_silva09_3, ev_food_security_wocat_1595_2013_risk_of_production_failure]. Neither source measures income change, and the Brazilian null concerns cash income rather than other welfare outcomes.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Capturing roof runoff in a tank keeps it off the ground around the homestead: the Ugandan Rubagano sheet rates surface runoff as reduced, and the Nepali compiler notes less eroded material from the courtyard [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1595_2013_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1497_2011_downstream_siltation].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Both units are practitioner ratings, and the Nepali sheet rates downstream siltation unchanged despite its comment, so any effect is confined to the homestead and is not measured [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1497_2011_downstream_siltation]. Runoff reduction and sediment retention enter only as component proxies for soil erosion.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The Nepali rooftop rainwater harvesting sheet rates downstream siltation unchanged, while its compiler notes less eroded material from the courtyard [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1497_2011_downstream_siltation].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This rests on a single practitioner rating of downstream siltation, a component proxy; it says nothing about the quality of the stored water itself [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1497_2011_downstream_siltation].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Domestic rooftop cisterns store rainwater beside the house, giving households basic drinking and cooking water through the dry season, sharply reducing time spent fetching water and dependence on water trucks [ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_1, ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_1, ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_4]. The Ugandan Rubagano sheet rates water quantity as greatly increased [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1595_2013_water_quantity].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Most units come from cistern programmes in Brazil (upper-middle income), largely programme authors and household surveys. A standard cistern covers basic needs only for small households, larger families remain dependent on water trucks, and most households still use other sources as their main supply [ev_water_access_deficit_brito07_1, ev_water_access_deficit_arsky20_2, ev_water_access_deficit_silva09_2]. The Ugandan sheet rates overall water availability only slightly improved [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1595_2013_water_availability].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In a Kenyan supplemental-irrigation trial, the poor rainfall of the SR98 season generated very little runoff, and the tarpaulin-lined earth dam that fed the irrigation barely contained any water [ev_climate_shock_barr05_6]. Drought disables a runoff store by leaving it empty: with nothing to harvest, the work cannot deliver water when the crop needs it.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row rests on that Kenyan observation alone. It records the reservoir running dry, not physical damage to the dam, and gives no measure of how often or how badly storage works fail in drought; records of drought-season performance or damage at further sites are needed before the row can say how sensitive runoff storage is [ev_climate_shock_barr05_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Heavy rain slightly damages runoff-catchment works such as check dams. A review of check-dam studies notes that failures are common worldwide and often linked to structures breaking in extreme rain or to lack of maintenance [ev_climate_shock_luca21_1_av]. Practitioners rate gully-plugging check dams in Nepal as not coping well with local rainstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1493_2011_local_rainstorm], gabions and rock check dams in Somalia as coping only moderately with rainstorms and thunderstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_7778_2026_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_7778_2026_local_thunderstorm], and brushwood check dams in Madagascar as coping moderately with hailstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_6478_2022_local_hailstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Most works are rated as coping well: gabion check dams in Tunisia, check dams in China, sand dams in Kenya, stone check walls in India and brushwood check dams in Madagascar under rainstorms and thunderstorms [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1400_2011_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1455_2011_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1537_2012_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_5210_2019_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_6478_2022_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_6478_2022_local_thunderstorm]. Apart from a review statement, which does not separate rain damage from neglect [ev_climate_shock_luca21_1_av], all the evidence is practitioner ratings, not measured damage.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The WOCAT compiler for stone check walls and check dams in India records that the technology copes well with forest fire [ev_asset_fire_wocat_5210_2019_forest_fire].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state how sensitive these structures are to fire: one practitioner rating, with no observed damage, no stated reasoning and no fire event described [ev_asset_fire_wocat_5210_2019_forest_fire]. It does not show the works go undamaged. What is missing is a second independent source or one observed account of fire damage or its absence.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Check dams and similar runoff-catchment structures can be overwhelmed by large floods. In Ethiopia, boulder-faced log check dams designed to resist abrasive flows still had 37.9% fail after a high-magnitude runoff event [ev_check_dam_failure_fran21_2]. On China's Loess Plateau, a single large flood — more than 200 mm of rain — damaged 20% of the main check dams in the Wuding River watershed [ev_climate_shock_shi19_3].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Not every structure is equally exposed: in Tunisia, a project reported its structure copes well with general river flooding [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1400_2011_general_river_flood], and in Ethiopia a different project reported coping very well with flash flooding [ev_asset_flood_wocat_6716_2023_flash_flood]. Part of this effect is off-site (downstream or landscape scale) rather than on the adopting farm.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The WOCAT compiler for gabions and rock check dams in Somalia rates the technology as coping moderately with heatwaves [ev_asset_heat_stress_wocat_7778_2026_heatwave].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single practitioner rating with no stated reason or observed damage [ev_asset_heat_stress_wocat_7778_2026_heatwave].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Stone check walls and check dams in India are rated by their WOCAT compiler as coping moderately with landslides [ev_asset_landslide_wocat_5210_2019_landslide], and a double-basin masonry check dam in Ethiopia as coping well [ev_asset_landslide_wocat_6716_2023_landslide].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This rests on just these compiler ratings from technology sheets; neither reports how a landslide would damage the structure, so there is no measured evidence on landslide damage to runoff-catchment works [ev_asset_landslide_wocat_5210_2019_landslide, ev_asset_landslide_wocat_6716_2023_landslide].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Sediment trapped behind water-harvesting structures slowly fills them, so they lose storage and soak up less water; the damage is real but builds up slowly, so it is rated slight. Sedimentation is described as perhaps the main reason sand dams fail [ev_asset_failure_ritc21_3]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, dams designed to last 30 years were set to fill in 4.4 to 5.7 years [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_1], and 50% of Ethiopian reservoirs studied were on course to lose their useful life before half their design period [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_2]. In Zambia, 8 of 10 reservoirs lost storage to silt and 3 lost over half their capacity [ev_asset_siltation_saru19_4]; 61% of Tigray micro-dams had benefits threatened by silt [ev_climate_shock_gebr18_5]; and in India 31% of earthen dams silted up within five years [ev_erosion_hazard_iegind11_12]. Check dams filled to more than 80% of their capacity within four years in Arizona [ev_sediment_retention_poly14_1_av] and fill quickly under heavy sediment loads in China [ev_climate_shock_shi19_4]; small Moroccan hill dams lose 0.5 to 1% of their capacity each year [ev_sediment_retention_roos10_1_av]. Silt on the floor of check dams and percolation tanks in India lowers how much water soaks into the ground [ev_climate_shock_dash17_4, ev_climate_shock_mass14_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_glen12_11_av].
